items.title: Bill Huntington and Charlie Suhor Interview, 1992-04-06
items.q: that's where I first met Ellis.

ctx.x: So these are the people who I think others looked up to greatly as musical leaders. Nat Perillat, who died young, was a tenor saxist who people looked up to greatly. I didn't hear Ellis much in those days, not until the mid-fifties. He was in the Marine Corps. Is that why? Okay. But I mean the guys used to tell me, people like Richard Payne, you say, well we always get to get to Ellis' house and he said Ornette Coleman was there, you know, things like that.
Ellis was playing more tenor then actually. The first time I heard him he was playing tenor. I didn't know that. He was a very good tenor player.

Somebody I should mention just because he is sort of a grandparent-like link with so many of the players of the time is a drummer named Lou Dillon, who's now the retiring business agent. He was a damn good teacher. He played some jazz well, played Latin music, played show drums, a good show drummer. But he taught Reed Vaughn when Reed was just kind of bumping around trying to find a style. I know Lou. He's nice. Okay. Reed then said you've got to take lessons from this guy I'm taking from, because Reed was…
